articles.title_zh: White House blocks CNN from traveling with Trump on Air Force One
articles.content_orig:
The White House on Friday night removed CNN from joining President Donald Trump on his trip to Tennessee on Saturday, where it was supposed to cover the president on behalf of major TV networks.
According to media guidance sent out by the White House on Friday night, CNN was removed from the list of outlets designated for pool coverage of Trump’s trip, in which he is set to attend a college football game in Knoxville.
The pool is a rotating group of networks that share duties of filming the president both in Washington and on official trips. Other member networks — Fox News, ABC News, CBS News and NBC News — briefly boycotted participating in the pool this week after Trump banned CNN from serving as a member.
CNN on Friday reported that it had been scheduled to fly with Trump on Air Force One on Saturday as part of its pool duties covering the president’s trip to the game between the University of Texas and the University of Tennessee. However in the president’s schedule released Friday night, CNN was not listed as a member of the pool and no other network was listed as replacing it.
The move is the latest development in the White House’s attempt to restrict access by CNN and other outlets to cover the White House. The president last week had banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico from accessing the White House before a judge temporarily blocked that move Thursday and ordered the administration to restore their reporters’ credentials for 14 days.
But while the order restored the outlets’ access to the White House, it didn’t explicitly require the administration to restore CNN’s participation in the television pool.
The White House did not immediately return a request for comment.
Casey Wooten is a breaking news editor for the politics team at NBC News.

articles.content_orig:
President Trump has rejected the latest proposal from Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in seven days and launch in-depth negotiations to end the war.
"I'm rejecting their deal," Mr. Trump told reporters while leaving the White House on Saturday to travel to Tennessee. "They want to make a deal where they open the strait immediately because they are losing so badly. You don't see that in the fake news. We're winning tremendously, we have total control of the Hormuz Strait, massive amounts of oil are coming out of the Hormuz Strait, last night we had 29 ships come out."
"They want to make a deal," he continued. "I think that's fine, I like making a deal too. But that deal [they offered] would not be acceptable."
Both the U.S. and Iran had expressed optimism over talks held in New York during the U.N. General Assembly, though they were short on details of what was discussed. Mr. Trump did not attend the talks directly, but his son-in-law, Jared Kushner, and special envoy Steve Witkoff were involved in the negotiations with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.
The deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz was reportedly similar to the Islamabad memorandum signed in June, including ending the blockade, allowing Iranian oil sales and halting fighting in every Middle East theater. The U.S. disputed Iran's interpretation of the MOU over who controlled traffic in the strait and the deal fell apart by July.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian had told CBS News' Margaret Brennan on Friday that his country was standing at the ready to implement the new deal.
"If this message reaches the president of the United States, or the interviewers and those involved in the discussions, naturally the process will begin from the very day they accept it," he said.
China pushed back against the United States in its speech at the U.N. General Assembly on Saturday, saying sovereignty of countries in the Gulf should be respected.
Vice President Han Zheng did not mention the U.S. by name in his remarks.
The comments stood in sharp contrast to the friendship on display earlier this week at the White House, where President Trump feted Chinese leader Xi Jinping with military flyovers and at a lavish state dinner.
"Major countries should have special responsibilities for safeguarding international peace and security, and they should take the lead in complying with the rules, upholding rule of law, and doing what's right," Han said.
"China holds that the sovereignty and security of countries in the Middle East, including the Gulf, should be respected," he added.
Trump warned Xi against providing support to Iran during the Washington talks and received assurances that China would not do so, the U.S. ambassador to China said on Friday.
The warning followed reports Beijing had supplied Iran with shoulder-fired air-defense missile launchers and Tehran had found ways to evade sanctions on its oil sales with Chinese help.
Iran will not resort to violence in order to counter harsh sanctions against its airline industry imposed by the United States, according to Maj. Gen. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, as told to semi-official ISNA news agency.
Rezaei issued a statement on steps Iran will take to address the sanctions after it was reported on Friday , based on comments by an adviser to the country's supreme leader, that Iran would shut down airspace in the Middle East through military action.
He said Iran would not respond with military retaliation as was falsely reported.
"Negotiations between Iran and the countries concerned to lift some of the illegally imposed air restrictions are being pursued and followed up seriously," according to a statement.
It continued, "There are multiple non-military options for retaliation that will be implemented, if necessary, with regard to some airports. We hope, of course, that the matter does not reach this point."
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said earlier this week that Iranian airlines would "shut down" from Wednesday, and he threatened countries that allowed them to use their airports with expulsion from the U.S. dollar system .
Wall Street has a busy week ahead with important updates on inflation, the jobs market and consumer confidence.
The reports could help provide a clearer picture on how consumers are handling higher prices on a wide range of products and services.
On Wednesday, the U.S. will release a key inflation report, the personal consumption expenditures price index, for August. The PCE is closely monitored by Wall Street and the Federal Reserve.
Inflation remains stubbornly above 3% and the Federal Reserve recently raised interest rates in an effort to tame high prices. The central bank has a target rate for inflation of 2%.
High gasoline prices have been fueling a broader jump in inflation, squeezing household budgets and sapping consumer confidence. The U.S. war with Iran has stifled global oil supplies since late February. It has a direct impact via higher gasoline prices, but higher fuel costs also make shipping more expensive. That raises prices for everything from food to clothing.
President Masoud Pezeshkian has departed New York for Tehran after the annual U.N. gathering of world leaders, semi-official media outlets in Iran reported.
Pezeshkian's speech to the gathering pushed back against Trump's latest threat to "annihilate" the Islamic Republic, but he ended by saying Tehran remains open to diplomacy.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told journalists Friday night that under Tehran's latest proposal, Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume talks on its nuclear program in seven days if the United States lifts its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waives sanctions on Iranian oil sales and observes a ceasefire that would include Lebanon.
President Trump has rejected that proposal, according to The Wall Street Journal . The White House has not officially commented on the deal, though the president posted "IRAN CAN NOT HAVE A NUCLEAR WEAPON!!!" on Truth Social on Saturday morning.
The Iraqi government said Saturday it was holding talks with the United States to secure an exemption from the ban on Iranian airlines.
All Iraqi airports enforced the ban this week, resulting in major disruption at the airport of the holy city of Najaf, the main destination for Iranian flights to Iraq.
"The Iraqi government is holding direct talks with the American side to exempt certain Iraqi airports from these measures," the prime minister's media office said.
An exemption would allow flights to resume "for humanitarian reasons, including medical treatment, education, religious visits, and for the interest of civilians," it added.
Iranian airlines mainly carry Iraqi Shia pilgrims to Iran's holy cities or Iranians visiting sacred sites in Iraq. The flights also serve Iraqi students studying in Iran and patients seeking medical treatment there.
Iraq has joined several countries including the United Arab Emirates in enforcing the US ban, after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Iranian airlines would be "shut down" on Wednesday.
Relations between between Iraq and neighbouring Iran, both Shia-majority countries, have long been close, due to religious kinship as well as political and economic interests.

However, U.S. officials quoted by The Wall Street Journal reportedly said Mr. Trump is "skeptical" Iran would meet his demands and that he expects to resume a bombing campaign.

articles.title_orig: Third suspect arrested in death of Mississippi woman found hanging at ‘staged’ crime scene
articles.title_zh: Third suspect arrested in death of Mississippi woman found hanging at ‘staged’ crime scene
articles.content_orig:
Warning: This story contains distressing details
Police in the US state of Mississippi have said they believe a black woman was already dead before her body was "staged" by being placed hanging in a tree.
The disclosure was made in court by a detective on Friday, who also said they believed Tasia Fortune, a mother of four, had been killed in a dispute related to drugs.
The 29-year-old's body was found hanging from a tree at an abandoned home in Jackson in August.
The discovery sparked widespread fears in the majority-black city, due to the state's deep history of racial violence and lynchings. After weeks of speculation and demands for information, police made multiple arrests.
Police said that the medical examiner had determined that Fortune's death was a homicide and that "the scene and the hanging were staged".
Officials have not stated the exact cause of death or shared why they believe the hanging may have been staged.
Fortune's mother told the BBC that she remembered the coroner telling her: "We're not treating this as [an] actual hanging." Her daughter, they told her, was dead before being placed in the tree.
Christy Spivey also recalled police telling her the incident was "drug related".
She described how she knew her daughter fought for her life till the very end while speaking to reporters outside the Jackson Police Department on Friday.
"I know she did. I know my daughter," Spivey said, adding that Fortune had left behind four young children, aged seven, five, four and one.
Dressed in a shirt that read "Justice for Tasia Fortune", Spivey stressed that she did not want to see any innocent people going to jail.
"I just hope they have the right people," she said.
Three people have so far been arrested in relation to the case, all of whom are black, including Jarques Ratliff, 51, who has pleaded not guilty. He remains in custody without bail.
A second person, Earnest Lloyd Jr, 25, was arrested in relation to the case this week.
A third, 45-year-old Eric Clark, turned himself in to authorities on Friday and was charged with murder. He is scheduled to appear in court on Monday.
The 29-year-old's death is one of several cases in recent years that has prompted lawmakers to call on the justice department and the FBI to investigate all hanging deaths of black people in the country.
Representative Ayanna Pressley, a Democrat from Massachusetts, cited at least 10 documented incidents in her September letter to Congress , external , which contained over 50 signatures from US lawmakers.
The most recent incident happened in Prince George's County, a majority-black suburb near Washington DC, on Sunday. It has since been ruled a suicide.

articles.title_orig: Hurricane Nolo expected to bring heavy rain as it skirts Hawaii’s Big Island
articles.title_zh: Hurricane Nolo expected to bring heavy rain as it skirts Hawaii’s Big Island
articles.content_orig:
NAALEHU, Hawaii — Hurricane Nolo is forecast to strengthen into a major hurricane in the Pacific Ocean over the weekend and unleash intense rain, the possibility of life-threatening flash flooding and dangerous surf for Hawaii’s Big Island.
Nolo was a Category 5 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 160 mph early Saturday, the National Hurricane Center said, as its outer rainbands hit the Big Island. Hurricane conditions are possible on the island, especially in areas with steep terrain, the weather service warned.
The storm was moving north-northwest at 10 mph on Saturday morning, but was expected to turn northeast and head toward Baja California Sur on Monday.
This marks the third hurricane in less than two months to whip past Hawaii (following Lala and Lowell ). The active Pacific hurricane season is likely due to a record-setting El Niño — a natural climate pattern characterized by a rise in sea surface temperatures in the eastern Pacific, which can spawn more intense and frequent cyclones there.
Tess Kala, a South Point resident who grew up in the area, said the back-to-back storms are a shock to locals.
“Honestly, this is the first like, whoa, what happened? We had a lot of family and friends that have lived here all their lives through generations and never experienced this before,” she said.
Hawaii Gov. Josh Green said Friday that President Donald Trump approved the state’s request for an emergency declaration to provide federal assistance for emergency protective measures across the state.
Mark Peters, a resident of seven years of Naalehu, on the Big Island’s southern tip, said the damage from the recent hurricanes has not been forgotten.
“It hurts me when I see friends and neighbors and people of this community that I know, and I just see it in their eyes, I hear it in their voices. We’ve been through a lot down here, and we still got a lot to go,” Peters said.
“We’re just getting started with our recovery. But to have yet another big storm hit us, and potentially even bigger than the last one, it’s difficult,” he said.
While he praised his community for its resilience, he said the people are still in need of basics like food and water, and many are in the process of reconstruction.
“We’re talking years. This is going to be a long recovery,” Peters said Friday.
He recalled driving through Waiohinu in the aftermath of Hurricane Lala and his “eyes getting wide open with all the damage, and the cars and houses moved and not where they’re supposed to be, and Waiohinu Park having buildings in the baseball field.”
Kala, the South Point resident, is preparing for Nolo by “moving everything away from the houses, tying things down, making sure that everything is hosed up and taped up as best as we possibly can.”
Nolo will bring periods of heavy rain that will continue across the Big Island and Maui over the weekend, and could trigger life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in steep terrain across eastern and southern portions of both the Big Island and Maui, the hurricane center said.
Nolo is forecast to dump 8 to 12 inches of rain on the eastern and southern parts of the Big Island, with maximum amounts up to 16 inches. Western portions of the Big Island could see 1 to 3 inches of rain, with maximum amounts of 6 inches. Meanwhile, Maui could see 4 to 6 inches, with maximum amounts of 8 inches, the National Hurricane Center said.
The rest of Hawaii will experience smaller rainfall totals, but isolated flooding is possible.
Nolo could also bring large and damaging waves along portions of the Big Island’s coastline into the weekend.
A hurricane watch and tropical storm warning are in effect for Hawaii County, and a tropical storm watch is in effect for Maui County. A hurricane watch means that hurricane conditions are possible within 24-36 hours. A wind advisory has been issued for the rest of the state.
Tropical storm-force winds will reach the Big Island on Friday afternoon, with hurricane-force winds possible by late evening.
A high surf advisory is in effect for the south- and east-facing shores of the Big Island and the east-facing shores of Maui and Molokai. A high-surf advisory was also issued for the east-facing shores of Niihau, Kauai and Oahu beginning Friday evening.
Nolo could also spawn tornadoes and large waterspouts over and near the Big Island and to the right of the track of the tropical cyclone.
Marlene Lenthang reported from Los Angeles, and Ryan Chandler and Shanshan Dong reported from Naalehu, Hawaii.

George Russell held off Max Verstappen for his first win in three months to cut into Kimi Antonelli’s standings lead at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.
Russell started on pole and built a big lead before having to defend on two safety car restarts, before holding off Verstappen, who charged through the field from eighth to second and nearly chased down the Briton on the final lap.
Verstappen remains winless this year for the first time since his rookie season in 2016. Verstappen’s Red Bull teammate Isack Hadjar was third on his return from injury.
Antonelli started 16th after a crash in qualifying but ended up fifth as he limited the damage to his title lead, swerving to avoid a three-car crash ahead of him and later overtaking Lewis Hamilton.

A decent weekend for Haas, Red Bull and Lindblad. Williams should be happy with a point.
Too much for Russell to do but this performance should do wonders for his confidence. In fairness, he has driven well since the summer break.
“Win every race. My team-mate has had an incredible season, he’s been pretty flawless and now we’re getting to crunch time. I am going to focus on myself. It’s been a real tough period for me and I feel like I have come through the other side.”
“I am happy, it’s been very long six weeks. It’s been six weeks since I injured myself... this weekend I really too it step-by-step. It’s a track you can end up in the wall really quickly. It was a very slow build-up but it brought me here. I am very delighted.”
“We had a good race. The first stint was probably a bit difficult with the medium tyre but we worked out way into P3 and then we had a good restart... the yellow flag George lost a bit of boost in one corner. To the line I got close, but it was not enough.”
“It was amazing to be back on the top step of the podium. I want to say a big thank-you to my team. The first half of the race felt pretty plain sailing. All, in all incredible weekend. It’s just having more experience with this new driving style I’ve adopted. Every race since the break I feel like I’ve gone from strength to strength. I feel more like myself again.”

articles.title_zh: Athens explosion: Six dead in blast near Acropolis in Plaka district
articles.content_orig:
The building in the Plaka district was reduced to rubble strewn with household items
Six people have died, including a British national, in an explosion that destroyed a building housing a holiday rental property in the historic centre of Athens.
The blast on Friday happened in the Plaka area of the Greek capital, a neighbourhood close to tourist sites such as the Acropolis.
Four American holidaymakers were among the dead, along with a UK national and Greek national - reportedly an elderly couple who lived in the same building.
Pictures from the scene on Saturday showed emergency service workers searching through rubble, with a gas leak the suspected cause of the blast.
All six bodies had been recovered by Saturday afternoon. Athens Mayor Haris Doukas said: "We are talking about an incredible disaster."
The tourists were confirmed to be missing when they did not arrive for their flight at Athens airport later on Friday, Reuters news agency reported citing local police.
The three-storey building completely collapsed due to the force of the blast, with neighbouring buildings damaged and debris scattered across the road.
Investigators at the scene believe the blast was caused by a gas leak
Local media reported people were injured by material scattered across nearby streets and some buildings needed to be evacuated.
Excavators and thermal imaging cameras have been used at the scene to search for survivors.
The explosion happened on a small road situated between two of Athens' most visited sites - the Acropolis and the Temple of Olympian Zeus.
A UK Foreign Office spokesperson said: "We are aware of a suspected explosion in Athens and are in touch with the local authorities."

articles.title_orig: A 7-Day Standoff That Said So Much About Trump and the Media
articles.title_zh: A 7-Day Standoff That Said So Much About Trump and the Media
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON, D.C. (AP) – Journalists from three news outlets that President Donald Trump banned from White House grounds are back at the executive complex with TV cameras, laptops and microphones in hand.
But the legal battle between Trump and some of the media that cover him is far from over.
Here are some things to know about the White House press corps, lawsuits over press access, and the increasingly contentious relationship between the president and the Fourth Estate.
Last week, Trump said he was banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House over what he called unfavorable coverage and “fake news.” Some journalists with those organizations had their White House press passes revoked, prohibiting them from White House grounds.
The affected news organizations sued, and several other news outlets and press associations filed legal briefs and released statements supporting them.
RELATED | Idaho Congressman is only Republican publicly opposing Trump’s White House media ban
The president’s attorneys later argued in court that the outlets’ coverage threatened national security, but they didn’t detail how the coverage put the nation at risk. Court filings cited letters the administration sent each outlet outlining stories it found problematic and dangerous, but the judge found that the standard they described was too vague to justify the ban.
Attorneys for the news organizations called the ban a blatant First Amendment violation and a clear case of ‘viewpoint discrimination’ — government action that penalizes speech because of the viewpoint expressed.
U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly issued a temporary restraining order early Thursday, ordering the White House to reinstate the banned journalists’ press credentials. That order lasts 14 days.
There will likely be another round of court filings and legal arguments over the next several days before the judge decides whether to issue a longer-lasting ruling called a preliminary injunction.
Preliminary injunctions are also temporary, often designed to last until a lawsuit is resolved one way or another.
Kelly’s temporary order focused less on whether the news outlets enjoy a First Amendment free press right to White House access and more on whether their Fifth Amendment due process rights may have been violated.
Existing case law is clear, Kelly wrote. Members of the press corps are entitled to fair notice from the government about why their credentials may be revoked, as well as an opportunity to state their case to the government on why their credentials should be preserved.
Kelly wrote that he issued the temporary restraining order because it’s likely the news outlets will be able to demonstrate they weren’t given proper notice or a chance to respond.
The work of the president occurs around the clock and often in spaces too small to accommodate every journalist who covers the executive branch. The White House Correspondents’ Association — a group of journalists who cover the president — created the press pool decades ago to ensure that a rotating roster of journalists traveled with the president wherever he goes.
The pool typically follows the president almost everywhere, including aboard Air Force One, at state dinners, in the Oval Office and on the golf course. The pool traditionally represents print and wire reporters, photographers and radio and television journalists.
The effort is designed to hold the nation’s chief executive accountable on behalf of the American public, providing information on the president’s activities and the work of the executive branch. The pool is always near the president so journalists can document unexpected developments.
The pool distributes in-person reports and imagery to the broader press corps. They also share their notes, video and audio with other news outlets, congressional offices and interested parties.
The White House video pool consists of five major U.S. television broadcasters that take turns shooting and sharing video. When the White House banned CNN — which belongs to the pool — the other four pool members declined to participate in a show of solidarity. For days, the pool provided no live video of the president. By Friday, the video pool was back in operation.
For decades, the White House Correspondents’ Association selected the members of the pool, but that changed Feb. 25, 2025, when the White House announced its officials would pick the pool members — effectively giving the executive control over coverage of the American presidency.
The White House almost always selects journalists who are outwardly favorable to Trump as part of the mix.
To show his displeasure with a news organization’s coverage, Trump has hurled personal insults at journalists or tried to exclude outlets entirely. In some cases, the news organizations sue in response.
During Trump’s first term, the White House suspended the credentials of Jim Acosta, who was a CNN correspondent at the time. The same judge handling the lawsuit from CNN, MS NOW and Politico also decided Acosta’s case, ordering the White House to restore his credentials.
Last year, Trump barred Associated Press journalists from some events and kicked the news agency out of the press pool after it refused to accede to the president’s demands to change its style from “Gulf of Mexico” to “Gulf of America.”
AP sued, and that case is ongoing, though a preliminary ruling from a federal appeals court said Trump could ban the wire service from some highly restricted areas such as the Oval Office or Air Force One.
Boone reported from Boise, Idaho. Associated Press journalists Jocelyn Noveck in New York and Laurie Kellman in London contributed.

articles.title_orig: High Gas and Rising Mortgage Rates Trouble Trump as Midterms Near
articles.title_zh: High Gas and Rising Mortgage Rates Trouble Trump as Midterms Near
articles.content_orig:
Mortgage rates reached a grim milestone this week, topping 7% for the first time since January 2025 and reaching their highest level during either of Donald Trump’s presidential terms.
The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate climbed to 7.03% this week, up from 6.95% last week, according to data released Thursday by Freddie Mac.
It’s the fifth-straight week of rising mortgage rates, putting a deeper squeeze on housing affordability. Higher rates mean larger monthly payments and less purchasing power for buyers.
“Beyond the immediate financial constraints, the 7% threshold is a foreboding psychological barrier,” said Bright MLS chief economist Lisa Sturtevant. “Crossing this mark could create a chilling effect on the market, leading to home sales transactions to slow considerably this fall.”
However, mortgage rates remain well below the 7.79% peak they hit in 2023, when inflation was running at decades-high levels.
About seven months ago, the average 30-year mortgage rate briefly dipped below 6% for the first time in years, prompting hopes that cheaper borrowing would finally unfreeze the housing market. Instead, those hopes have faded as the war in Iran has pushed oil prices higher, adding fresh pressure to overall inflation and mortgage rates.
CNN Poll: Support for Iran War Collapsing | The Source with Kaitlan Collins | CNN Audio
Consider the difference between a homebuyer who locked in their mortgage rate in February, when the average briefly fell to 5.98%, and someone buying today. On a median-priced home with a 20% down payment, today’s buyer would pay hundreds of thousands of dollars more in interest over the life of a 30-year mortgage.
“Expect 7% as the new normal,” said Lawrence Yun, chief economist at the National Association of Realtors, in a blog post last week.
Action in the bond market is the chief cause for higher mortgage rates. US bond yields have climbed this year, pushing up interest rates across the economy.
The 10-year US Treasury yield is a benchmark for mortgage rates: They loosely track the 10-year, which moves with investors’ expectations for rate decisions by the Federal Reserve, but also inflation and growth expectations.
Know your bonds: A quick guide to Treasuries
As the 10-year yield has climbed this year, mortgage rates have pushed higher. And this week, the 10-year Treasury yield surged to its highest level in nearly two decades after fresh data on Wednesday pointed to a strong economy and intensifying inflation nerves.
The 10-year yield started the year at around 4.15%, and is now trading around 5.15%, its highest level since 2007. The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 6.16% at the start of the year.
Bond yields are rising as markets adjust to central banks starting to raise interest rates to tamp down inflation driven in large part by the energy shock caused by the Iran war.
The move higher in bond yields raises the cost of borrowing money, and some economists worry that yields have reached levels that could pose a risk for the broader economy.
Higher bond yields translate into higher mortgage rates, as well as auto loans, consumer loans and commercial loans.
When Trump left office in January 2021, the 30-year fixed mortgage rate was just below 2.8%.
A property developer and real estate investor himself, Trump placed the blame for the subsequent rise in mortgage rates squarely on the Fed’s shoulders. While mortgage rates don’t directly follow the central bank’s policy moves, Trump often berated former Fed Chair Jerome Powell for failing to lower the Fed’s benchmark interest rate quickly enough when inflation initially spiked during the early years of the pandemic.
Last week, Trump’s handpicked successor to Powell, Kevin Warsh, announced that the central bank hiked interest rates by a quarter point – its first hike since July 2023 – in an attempt to tamp down inflation. The central bank’s members have indicated they foresee at least one other rate hike in 2026.
On his social media platform Truth Social, Trump posted last week that “interest rates in the United States should be 1%, or less,” a significant drop from the Fed’s current rate range of 3.75% to 4%.
Higher rates are already starting to slow down the housing market.
Shares of some of the country’s largest homebuilders, including Lennar ( LEN ), D.R. Horton ( DHI ) and PulteGroup ( PHM ), have fallen over the past month as higher borrowing costs threaten to weigh on both home sales and new construction.
Last week, Lennar CEO Stuart Miller warned that many homebuyers are “clearly stretching” to afford to afford a home lately, attributing the company’s disappointing earnings to higher mortgage rates and stubborn inflation.
Although the pace of home sales have remained largely unchanged this year compared to last year, according to NAR data through August, there are some signs that higher mortgage rates have started scaring off some buyers.
Some homeowners have been waiting years for mortgage relief. It keeps slipping away
Pending home sales, which measure the number of homes under contract, rose 0.3% in August from July, but fell 4.7% from a year ago, according to the National Association of Realtors.
Mortgage applications to buy a new home fell 11% last week from the same week a year ago, according to Mortgage Bankers Association data released on Wednesday.
Among those still looking to buy, more borrowers are turning to adjustable-rate mortgages, or ARMs – a riskier loan product that played a role in the housing market’s buildup to the 2008 financial crisis.
Nearly 10% of borrowers opted for an ARM last week, according to the MBA. These loans typically offer a lower fixed rate for five, seven or 10 years before resetting with market rates. If rates are higher when the fixed period ends, borrowers can face sharply higher monthly payments.
Rates on 5/1 ARMs – which are fixed for five years and then adjust annually – were more than a percentage point lower than those for fixed-rate loans last week, said Mike Fratantoni, MBA’s chief economist.
Home prices have yet to reflect a national slowdown in demand, though. The median existing home price was $429,100 in August, the 38th consecutive month of year-over-year price increases, according to NAR.

articles.title_orig: Europe frets as the Kremlin pushes the limits of its hybrid warfare
articles.title_zh: Europe frets as the Kremlin pushes the limits of its hybrid warfare
articles.content_orig:
The Kremlin is testing Europe ‘s limits.
After months of covert attacks and sabotage across the continent, leaders are warning that Moscow may be about to grow bolder as it seeks to sow chaos and intimidate allies of Ukraine .
Russian President Vladimir Putin could try to test NATO’s resolve to defend members on its eastern flank or respond to attacks that fall short of all-out war, these officials say, at a time when the U.S. is distracted by other conflicts and weighing reducing its military presence in Europe.
An assessment by the Danish Defence Intelligence Service released Thursday warned that in the coming months Moscow will further intensify its campaign of so-called hybrid warfare , “with greater consequences for the targeted countries than in the past.” It also assessed “a low but growing risk that Russia will launch a limited military attack against one or several NATO countries bordering Russia.”
While Moscow has for years embraced tactics that straddle the threshold of war, a string of increasingly brazen incidents in recent months has alarmed U.S. allies.
A key moment was the discovery of a Russian drone carrying explosives at an airport in eastern Germany near a Ukrainian aircraft last month. Berlin formally blamed Russia for what it said was a thwarted attack and imposed a diplomatic freeze, though Moscow denied involvement.
That incident appears to have changed the mindset about Russia’s growing threat in Europe, said Ed Arnold, a senior associate fellow in international security at the Royal United Services Institute, a London-based think tank. “It just showed that Putin’s risk calculations are getting more liberal,” Arnold said. “Everyone just got a bit freaked out by that, quite frankly.”
It was followed by the unexpected visit of CIA Director John Ratcliffe to Moscow, during which NATO was discussed.
Incidents have continued to pile up — at defense facilities in Estonia, rail networks in Poland and the power grid in Germany. Many have passed without clear attribution, only intensifying speculation.
All this against the backdrop of near-daily drone incursions into European airspace, fueling anxiety in eastern border towns.
In Ukraine, a passenger train was hit less than 2 miles from the Polish border earlier this month, a close call on NATO’s doorstep that came as European diplomats returned from Kyiv on the same rail line. Another train, with former CIA Director David Petraeus on board, was still at the station when the drone struck.
Just days later, NATO fighter jets shot down a drone that entered the airspace of Lithuania, one of the Baltic member states whose proximity to Russia, analysts say, could make it a prime target for the Kremlin’s next move.
What could this look like? As unease increasingly swirled last week, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the Kremlin plans to launch drone and missile attacks against European countries that it would argue were accidental to try to weaken any response.
Russia has not claimed involvement in any of the incidents and has repeatedly denied conducting hybrid warfare or sabotage operations in NATO territory. Putin himself accused European leaders earlier this month of seeking out “a war against Russia” and “frightening their populations with an imaginary threat.”
On Friday, Russian state news agency RIA published and quickly deleted an op-ed laying out a potential scenario for a “lightning fast” war that Russia might wage against a NATO state, specifically focusing on the Baltic nations. The article was deleted because it did not “align” with editorial policy or Russia’s state policy, RIA said.
U.S. allies have little doubt that the broad pattern reflects the Kremlin increasingly pushing the boundaries.
“With these incidents now so frequent and so brazen, it is increasingly difficult to distinguish them from actual acts of war,” said Katja Bego, a senior research fellow with the Europe program at London-based think tank Chatham House. “The Kremlin is playing with fire here: The risk of more serious escalation — even if unintended — is very real.”
There is a mounting sense that something must be done, but what?
Lithuania has made plans for the evacuation of older adults and is lifting its ban on hosting nuclear weapons. Finland has warned citizens to be “mentally prepared” for new sabotage attacks. France is putting a plan in place to protect the country’s critical infrastructure.
Hanging over all of this is Article 5, NATO’s collective defense clause.
For Moscow, escalating hybrid attacks could highlight Western divisions over how best to respond and undermine the alliance at a time when the U.S. commitment to this mutual defense has been in question.
“I think they are trying to show Europe they can act without consequences, and more recently, to show Europe that the U.S. will not come to their rescue. It’s worrisome,” said William Alberque, a former senior NATO official based in Berlin.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov on Wednesday and told a media briefing that the U.S. was concerned that the Ukraine war could “metastasize and spread into other places ... be it through a hybrid attack, be it through a sabotage attack, be it through a misunderstanding.”
He added: “We watch reports carefully, and we raise them with the right people at the right levels.”
A State Department spokesperson told NBC News: “We continue to monitor Russia’s hybrid activities in Europe and are working closely with our allies and partners to strengthen resilience against the hybrid threat.”
Despite the spreading sense of alarm, some in Europe are urging against getting carried away.
NATO’s Baltic member states have not changed their security assessments, saying there is no imminent risk of a Russian invasion while much of Moscow’s military resources are tied up in Ukraine — and struggling to make progress there .
Latvia and Estonia directly border Russia, while Lithuania borders the Russian enclave of Kaliningrad. All three have been staunch supporters of Ukraine’s fight, driven in part by fears they could be next.
“Incursion of the type of 2022 Ukraine is not likely, let’s put it in a mild way,” Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs told reporters on the sidelines of this week’s United Nations General Assembly in New York. “Ukraine is fighting. Russia is absorbed in Ukraine. We do not observe any build-up near our borders,” Rinkēvičs added.
Neighboring Lithuania said this week a new rotation of U.S. troops was on its way to the country, ending uncertainty over a renewed deployment as the Pentagon weighs a broader plan to draw down U.S. forces on the continent.
“Russia’s pressure on Lithuania and other countries is not new,” Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas told NBC News, pointing to the decadelong Soviet occupation and adding that his country has more recently faced cyberattacks, disinformation and other forms of hostile influence from Moscow.
“There is no conventional threat at the moment,” Kaunas said via email, when asked why his country has not changed its security assessment. “At the same time, provocations and false-flag operations remain possible, and our intelligence points to increasingly aggressive Russian behavior. These are different threats, and they need different answers.”
But failing to take sufficient action could carry its own risks.
“Respond. Always respond,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged his European allies earlier this week.
“If you don’t respond to Russians, they will go further.”
Yuliya Talmazan is a reporter for NBC News Digital, based in London.

articles.title_orig: Inside Meta's months-long grind to turn Muse into a hit
articles.title_zh: Inside Meta's months-long grind to turn Muse into a hit
articles.content_orig:
A year ago, Meta was struggling to convince Silicon Valley that it could keep up in the AI race. Now it has one of the industry's hottest products.
Muse, Meta's new personal AI assistant, has rocketed to the top of the App Store and become a victory lap for CEO Mark Zuckerberg's massive AI spending. Meta's Connect conference this week was all about the app, which AI chief Alexandr Wang — who is 29 and has been posting risqué memes of Muse's mascot all week — called a "banger."
Getting there required months of painstaking work, a team led by former GitHub CEO Nat Friedman, and thousands of employees pulled from across Meta to teach the agent how to actually get things done, employees told Business Insider.
Meta also snapped up top AI agent talent through acqui-hires, including the leaders of Dreamer, an AI agent startup.
Whether Meta can sustain Muse's momentum is another question. Competitors like Instinct are thriving, and OpenAI is widely expected to launch a rival. Privacy concerns have also arisen, as Muse requires broad access to users' accounts to function. Meta employees are still reeling from a year of mass layoffs, employee surveillance, and low morale.
For now, at least, Muse's success — and a more than 20% increase in Meta's stock price since its launch — has become a morale boost, employees said. It also proves that Meta remains firmly in the AI race after being seen as a laggard a year ago.
"Muse is busy working for millions of people because of the hard work of a bunch of people at Meta — and we're still cooking," a Meta spokesperson said.
Muse's success was far from inevitable.
Since September 2025, Friedman, who heads the superintelligence unit's Products and Applied Research team , has been working hard on Muse, then codenamed "Hatch."
Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
As recently as two weeks before Muse's launch this month, the chatbot struggled with speaking good English, a person directly familiar with the matter said — and it came as a huge relief when it finally started scoring well on coherence tests.
Earlier this year, some of Meta's top AI employees were also worried about Muse, an employee told Business Insider. They had tried it out and found it working poorly — it felt like just another chatbot, but with a worse underlying AI model and extra steps, that person added.
Friedman's team eventually pulled it off. Tens of thousands of Meta employees tested Muse for months, coming up with a range of use cases for the agent, which became key to the effort.
That data helped Friedman's team improve Muse's ability to do things like book meetings and cancel plane tickets: the painful work of getting better at increasingly complex tasks, or "hill-climbing," as Silicon Valley calls it.
The team trained Muse to be considerate so that it didn't overshare, like telling people someone couldn't make a meeting because they were hungover, the person familiar said. Meta also focused on ensuring it could interact with the internet seamlessly by using tools it hadn't used before.
"Our researchers did a ton of work teaching agents how to choose the right tool for a job," Wang said this week at Connect.
Friedman's role was critical. Zuckerberg brought in the executive last year as part of a deal to buy a stake in his venture capital fund, NFDG. Last year, Friedman and Wang cowrote a memo outlining a "superintelligent personal sidekick" that would act as a trusted friend and advisor.
Friedman is unabashedly technical and hands-on. Internally, the executive is opinionated and proud of it, chafing with other teams across Meta's sprawling operations, one of the employees said. Meta's communications chief, Andy Stone, recently called him "Nat the Truthteller" after he derided a report about Muse's security as written by "dummies."
He also moves fast. His bare-bones personal website spells out his philosophy in characteristically blunt terms: "slow is fake" and "it's important to do things fast," it says. Friedman has pushed Meta's AI staff to ditch slow internal tools in favor of faster external ones, such as Vercel.
When the independent AI agent OpenClaw took the tech world by storm this winter, Friedman acted quickly. The free desktop-based tool was popular with developers, but mystifying to everyday users. Friedman aimed to build a far more accessible version from scratch.
He issued a two-page internal memo titled "The Claw Is The Law," praising the product, and also bought hundreds of Mac Minis for Meta's superintelligence team to run the agent.
While Muse is user-friendly now, making it all happen took "months of blood, sweat, and tears," the person familiar said.
Although it took a "long ass time," now it's something that anyone's "grandma can use," Wang later posted.
Meta also went on a hiring binge for researchers and engineers in agentic AI. It hired David Singleton and Hugo Barra, the cofounders of Dreamer, a startup helping people build their own agents, along with the rest of their team.
Singleton has worked on Muse since he began at Meta in March, helping design the core technology that enables the app to store sensitive information securely, he posted on X.
The efforts worked. Although the arrival of the viral AI agent Instinct initially upstaged Meta , Muse took off by tapping into Meta's enormous built-in audience across its apps — including among people who had never used AI agents before.
Meta wasn't the only one on a hiring spree. OpenAI hired OpenClaw's creator , Pete Steinberger, in a coup earlier this year. Meta was especially worried that it would be upstaged by a large competitor, the person familiar with the matter said, and the team was shocked as the months went by without such an entrant.
Wall Street is cheering on Muse, seeing it as a way for Meta to become more than an ad company. Zuckerberg told Alex Heath's Sources earlier this month that he wants people to shop and save money on Muse, which Meta plans to make money from by taking a small cut of each transaction.
"We see the Meta bull case increasingly playing out," Mizuho Americas analyst Lloyd Walmsley wrote in a note.
Users have praised how easy it is to set up Muse. Hadi Javeed, the cofounder of healthcare startup RevelAi, said his dad saw an ad for Muse in his Facebook feed and downloaded it, promptly using it to buy a new pair of shoes.
"They completely deleted all the setup that was required," Javeed said.
At the same time, Javeed, like many others, has raised data privacy concerns about Muse. By design, an app like Muse creates a new order of security and privacy risks, such as the app buying things without a user's permission. Privacy and trust remain key roadblocks to broader adoption of Muse, Bank of America analysts wrote.
Zuckerberg has said that the company held back Muse's launch due to safety and product liability concerns. He and Friedman also personally reached out to Signal creator Moxie Marlinspike to help co-design Muse's security architecture, Zuckerberg told Heath.
For now, Meta is on a high. The company has hinted that much more will come as it works on a new AI model, Watermelon. It says the model has already caught up with OpenAI. Wang says Meta has other ideas that are "just as big" as Muse.
"The kitchen is just getting warmed up," he posted on X.

articles.title_orig: Commanders announce Marcus Mariota will be a team captain for the rest of the season
articles.title_zh: Commanders announce Marcus Mariota will be a team captain for the rest of the season
articles.content_orig:
Marcus Mariota will be the Commanders’ starting quarterback for whatever games Jayden Daniels misses with his left elbow injury. And Mariota and Daniels will both be team captains for the rest of the season.
Commanders coach Dan Quinn announced on Friday that the five Commanders who were chosen as team captains before the season got together and decided they want Mariota to be a captain, not just while he’s the starting quarterback but also when he returns to the No. 2 job when Daniels returns.
“I thought it was such a cool thing: The captains huddled up with me earlier in week and said, ‘We’d like to make Marcus our sixth captain,’” Quinn said. “I thought, What a great tribute of brotherhood of those guys asking. They were all as on board as you could imagine. I thought it was awesome, too. What a great example of teammate and leadership.”
The Commanders say Mariota’s status as captain for the rest of the season is not an indication that he’ll be starting for long, as the team expects Daniels to be back soon. But even if Mariota spends most of the season on the bench, he’ll have the captain’s C on his jersey.
In addition to Mariota and Daniels, the Commanders’ captains are wide receiver Terry McLaurin, linebacker Frankie Luvu, safety Jeremy Reaves and punter Tress Way.

articles.title_zh: Chadwick Boseman's Family at War With His Widow Over Documentary She's Selling
articles.content_orig:
Chadwick Boseman 's widow, Taylor Simone Ledward Boseman , claims the late actor's family is making things difficult as she tries to work on a documentary celebrating his life.
According to court docs, obtained by TMZ, Simone says she has been working with production company Words + Pictures on a documentary about Chadwick.
She said she is in the process of securing an offer from Searchlight Pictures to produce the film. Simone said the deal is structured on a "Most Favored Nation basis," meaning it would ensure equal treatment for the family parties, and said, "both sides of the family were sent identical paperwork."
Simone claimed Chadwick's family members asked the production company for separate agreements. She calls it "yet another example of Simon's generosity to the Boseman family" because she says she retained "100% right to control and benefit from Chadwick's name, image, voice, signature, likeness etc."
Simone says she "has tried to consult with Chadwick's family at all times with respect to activities she has undertaken to honor Chadwick's legacy" ... but claims his family "has not done the same."
As TMZ first reported, Chadwick's brothers are trying to remove Simone as administrator of Chadwick's estate … claiming she has not been transparent about the finances.
Simone denies the claims and says she has gone above and beyond in working with the family … and has provided them with more money than was required.

articles.title_orig: We can’t stop the ‘Godzilla’ El Niño – but can we limit its damage?
articles.title_zh: We can’t stop the ‘Godzilla’ El Niño – but can we limit its damage?
articles.content_orig:
The ‘Godzilla’ El Niño is here, and it is already breaking records the world would rather have left unbroken.
Sea surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific Ocean have already surpassed the highest recorded during any previous El Niño, and the weather phenomenon is still strengthening. Between June 2026 and February 2027, experts estimate the extreme heat associated with it could contribute to 451,000 additional deaths.
The forecast has set off alarm bells among weather agencies, health authorities and governments around the world, including an unprecedented mobilisation by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) to prepare for the extreme weather ahead.
“El Niño is being supersized before our eyes,” outgoing UN Secretary-General António Guterres said in early September. “The planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up.”
But even as governments brace for what could be a devastating year of extreme weather, experts say there is still plenty that can be done to limit the damage – both now and in the future.
Records aside, many worry about what an El Niño of this strength could mean for weather around the world in the months ahead.
An El Niño event starts in the Pacific, but its effects can be felt around the world. When waters near the equator become unusually warm, they release heat into the atmosphere, pushing up global temperatures and changing where rain falls.
With ocean temperatures already at record highs, this El Niño could bring more intense heat, drought and heavy rainfall in vulnerable regions and push global temperatures to new highs – earning it the nicknames ‘Godzilla’ and ‘Super’ El Niño.
Some of those effects are already being felt . India has already experienced below-normal monsoon rainfall while southern Africa faces an increased risk of drought.
Even though Europe is unlikely to experience the most severe direct effects, El Niño can influence winter weather, and droughts or failed harvests elsewhere can disrupt supplies of foods imported into Europe.
The threat is already prompting governments to act around the world. This month, California Governor Gavin Newsom preemptively declared a state of emergency to prepare for potential flooding, landslides, coastal erosion and powerful winter storms.
For all the preparations we make, one thing remains unavoidable: El Niño is a natural phenomenon. But even if we can’t prevent it, forecasts give us months to prepare.
“The key is to manage water and prepare for the changes in where and when rainfall occurs,” says Davide Faranda, research director at France’s National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) and a lead author for the UN’s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).
For example, he explains, governments can store and distribute water more carefully, better control how reservoirs and underground water are used, adjust farming schedules and irrigation practices, and prepare communities for droughts or floods.
The FAO has also offered concrete advice . Farmers, FAO officials say, can reduce losses by changing planting dates, irrigating at cooler times of day, storing water ahead of droughts and taking steps to protect their crops and livestock from extreme heat.
Some governments have stepped up with financial support.
The UK has pledged up to £15 million (€17 million) to help vulnerable countries prepare for this El Niño. The money will fund measures that range from vaccinating livestock before droughts to reinforcing homes before flooding and providing farmers with cash before harvests fail.
Most El Niño events increase global average temperatures by around 0.2°C. While this is enough to trigger extreme weather conditions across the Global South, it is a fraction of the additional warming caused by climate change.
The burning of fossil fuels has pushed global average surface temperatures by approximately 1.3°C to 1.4°C above pre-industrial levels, paving the way for Europe’s scorching summer that triggered mass droughts and wildfires.
El Niño’s impacts are therefore compounded by an already warming world. It’s why 2025 was the third warmest year on record – hotter than the El Niño year of 2016 – despite the naturally forming cool drag of a La Niña event.
Recent research suggests that climate change is turbocharging El Niño as well. A study published in August found that El Niños are 36 per cent stronger than before the industrial era, a trend researchers linked to human-caused warming.
If climate change is making El Niño stronger, then preparation will only go so far. But Faranda says cutting emissions can make a big difference over the long term.
A hotter planet means more extreme heat, more strain on water supplies and, in some places, more rainfall. Reducing emissions would not stop the natural climate cycle that leads to El Niños, he explains, but it would reduce the human-caused warming that is making those threats more severe.
That means the damage is not entirely beyond our control. “We cannot eliminate El Niño through climate mitigation,” Faranda says, “but we can reduce the extent to which climate change makes its consequences more severe.”

articles.title_orig: TikTok to pay Alabama $100m and limit teenage use in first state settlement
articles.title_zh: TikTok to pay Alabama $100m and limit teenage use in first state settlement
articles.content_orig:
Trial had been set for Monday over claims by Alabama that TikTok misled parents about tools meant to shield children from harmful content
TikTok has agreed to pay Alabama at least $100m and enact time limits and other restrictions for teenage users, avoiding a trial with a settlement that was modelled on Instagram-owner Meta’s recent agreement with US states.
Alabama described it as a “first-in-the-nation settlement” with a state in the sweeping litigation over social media’s affect on teen wellbeing.
A trial had been set to begin on Monday in the southern US state over claims by Alabama that TikTok misled parents about tools meant to shield children from harmful content.
TikTok’s settlement with Alabama mirrors safety provisions agreed by Meta, including a two-hour daily time limit for teens, restricted access from midnight to 6am, and suspending notifications during school hours.
It will also strengthen age verification, ban beauty filters for teenagers, and offer young users a non-personalised content feed.
Attorney general Steve Marshall hailed Friday’s settlement as “a great day for Alabama parents”. He said: “Tonight, they can rest easier knowing real protections are in place to shield their children from the dangers of social media addiction.”
Under the settlement, TikTok will send $100m to Alabama and could possibly pay up to $300m in total if 40 other attorneys general sign similar agreements with the company within a specified timeframe.
Alabama’s suit was the latest in a wave of litigation targeting social media companies across the United States about alleged harm their apps cause young users.
In August, Meta agreed to pay $18bn to settle a sweeping lawsuit brought by US states accusing it of designing Instagram and Facebook to get children addicted.
In addition, the Alabama deal includes a conditional restriction that Meta also agreed to: expanding the night-time shutdown period to 10pm to 7am if other platforms also commit to do the same.
“TikTok’s priority has always been fostering a safe and positive space where people can be creative, discover what they love, and connect with their community,” a company spokesperson told AFP.
“This builds on our commitment and core objective to continually enhance our robust safety tools to protect teens,” the spokesperson added.
More than a dozen other states, including California and New York, still havesuits against TikTok.
The company has previously settled cases against it that were headed for trial, including a Los Angeles lawsuit brought by a young woman and a suit from a Kentucky school district.
Meta, by contrast, has taken its chances in court – with bruising results.
In March, a jury in New Mexico ordered the Facebook and Instagram owner to pay $375m after finding it had misled the public about the safety of its platforms for children.
That same month, a Los Angeles jury found Meta and Google’s YouTube negligent in the case of a 20-year-old woman who said she became hooked on social media as a child, awarding her $6m.
Going to trial would have exposed TikTok to unprecedented public scrutiny of how it handles safety, with company documents and executive testimony potentially aired in open court.
Alabama originally sued TikTok and its Chinese parent company ByteDance in April 2025, alleging the app was engineered to hook young users “just like a sophisticated gambling machine”.
The state later narrowed its case to claims under Alabama’s Deceptive Trade Practices Act, focusing on whether TikTok misrepresented the effectiveness of features such as “Restricted Mode” and “Kids Mode.”
The lawsuit accused TikTok of falsely claiming it limits access to sexual and violent content for young users to have its app rated safe for teens in app stores run by Google, Apple and Microsoft and of misleading users about the Chinese government’s access ‌to US users’ data.
TikTok said it designed its platform with teen safety as a key priority and argued that section 230 of the federal Communications Decency Act shields online platforms from liability for user-generated content.

articles.title_orig: ‘To Catch a Predator’ Host Chris Hansen Watches Robert Pattinson’s ‘Primetime’ — and He’s Not a Fan
articles.title_zh: ‘To Catch a Predator’ Host Chris Hansen Watches Robert Pattinson’s ‘Primetime’ — and He’s Not a Fan
articles.content_orig:
Former To Catch a Predator host Chris Hansen was interviewed on his podcast Friday to give his unfiltered reaction to A24 ‘s unauthorized, dramatized film about parts of his life, Primetime , which he called overly dramatic, detached from reality, and a “fever dream” — while giving Robert Pattinson ‘s performance a “D” grade.
Primetime , which opens Friday in the U.S., is set in 2006 and follows Pattinson’s fictionalized version of Hansen as the popular To Catch a Predator segment on NBC’s Dateline grows into its own primetime block on the network. On the show, Hansen blurred journalistic lines by working with law enforcement and the watchdog group Perverted Justice to intercept adult men as they arrived, unbeknownst to them, at a sting house to meet a minor they’d met online for sex. The men were typically arrested as a result. The series drew mixed reactions, with concerns about potential entrapment-law violations at the forefront of the criticism.
In a brief segment produced for his video podcast, Have a Seat with Chris Hansen , the former NBC News journalist is seen exiting a Times Square AMC after viewing the film for the first time at a Thursday night screening — his first look at the indie drama since its theatrical release. He’s then asked for his first reaction to the Lance Oppenheim-directed film .
“It’s hard for me to — obviously, I’m not a judge, because the character is based on me,” he said. “I think because the character is so detached from reality, from anything I’ve ever experienced then or now doing the investigations — I’m not sure what the point of it was.”
The rest of the podcast episode has Hansen discussing the film, its director and Pattinson’s portrayal of him with Fox News’ Jesse Watters. Hansen railed against the movie throughout.
Oppenheim has said he conceived Primetime after receiving a personalized Cameo video from the To Catch a Predator host. Hansen said on his podcast that he spoke to a mutual friend before seeing the film, and that Oppenheim told the friend it was “something to the effect of, ‘a love letter to Chris Hansen, and it gets a little weird in the storytelling.'”
Hansen also flagged inaccuracies in the fictionalized version of his life — including scenes involving Jeff Zucker and Stone Phillips that he insists never happened — and said absolutely nothing in the film was close to reality. He assured viewers he’s not the ratings-obsessed figure the script conjures. His biggest gripe, he said, is that the film portrays him as an aloof parent, which he says is far from how he relates to his kids. As for Pattinson’s take on Hansen circa 2006, Hansen had few kind words.
“He’s got work to do. I’m kind of the only guy that counts for this, right?” he said.
Days before seeing the movie, Hansen spoke with The Hollywood Reporter ‘s Seth Abramovich about what he knew of the film. A24 hadn’t reached out to him or the production to explain the premise or ask for his input, he said.
“Based upon what I’ve seen in the trailer and my understanding of what’s been written about the film, they wanted to create something much darker and way more dramatic,” he said. “I think it’s an insult to the thousands of men and women who work hard every day to protect children from predators. They’ve turned something that is very positive, very challenging and not without risk into what is essentially a horror film.”
On Friday, after viewing Primetime , he doubled down with a direct swipe at Oppenheim.
“You have to question the motives of not coming forward and talking to me or anybody I’ve worked closely with over the years,” he said. “They didn’t want to hear that Chris Hansen is a good guy. They didn’t want to hear that this work is important. This director had a dark image of what he wanted to do. He wanted to create a horror-like film with interesting photography, and didn’t want to hear anything else.”
Hansen continues identifying and capturing potential child predators on Takedown with Chris Hansen . Earlier on Friday, Hansen’s TruBlu streaming network dropped the trailer for I’m Chris Hansen , a documentary centered around the host.

articles.title_orig: All the Major Social Media Networks Are Reportedly Refusing Ads for ‘Musk’
articles.title_zh: All the Major Social Media Networks Are Reportedly Refusing Ads for ‘Musk’
articles.content_orig:
Senior Editor, Technology and Politics
So much for free speech. The studio releasing Alex Gibney ’s new Elon Musk documentary Musk is finding itself unable to buy an ad on the biggest social platforms. YouTube , TikTok , and Instagram and Facebook owner Meta are all declining to run the trailer for Musk , along with X itself, The Hollywood Reporter has learned. That last one is perhaps understandable, given its owner. But the rejection by the other platforms has taken distributor Bleecker Street by surprise, and it is internally scrambling to understand why the ad has been rejected, according to a person familiar with the company’s processes who is not authorized to talk about them publicly. The unwillingness of platforms to accept even paid advertising is sure to raise concerns about free speech and the dwindling number of companies that control many of the platforms in this country — and ironically provide a proof-text for the very point the film is coming to make. Gibney’s doc is a four-hour look at a title character who attempts to control the conversation in various ways , including with alleged suppressions on X, which he bought in 2022.
Bleecker Street opens Musk in theaters on Oct. 9. YouTube, TikTok and Meta have all supplied a reason related to “political content” to Bleecker Street reps. The latter two companies’ platforms, by policy, do not allow campaign or other political ads, in Meta’s case largely owing to fallout from the Cambridge Analytica Facebook scandal during the 2016 election. But the Musk trailer, which dropped Thursday, does not appear to fall in the category of the campaign advertising those bylaws were enacted to prevent. It simply contains a shot of a political rally in 2024 and a reference at the end to the 2024 election — the kind of flicks that occur in numerous documentaries and are hardly meant to stump for a particular candidate in an upcoming race.
The reason for YouTube’s rejection is even less clear, as the platform does allow campaign ads, albeit with “paid for” disclosures from vetted candidates.
Bleecker Street has entered an appeal with all three companies. Meta has already rejected the appeal. TikTok and YouTube are still entertaining the petitions. For its part, X has refused to engage with Bleecker Street on the film or even accept advertising for any of its other films on its upcoming calendar. Press reps at Meta, TikTok, YouTube and X did not immediately provide a comment. A Bleecker Street representative confirmed that the ads were initially rejected but said they are continuing to appeal with all three companies besides X in the hope minds can be changed.
Traction on social media is key for a documentary release, which relies on word-of-mouth in a way a big-budget feature doesn’t.
The news also hits a nerve after Universal, which is releasing the film overseas, considered backing away from distributing Musk before capitulating to public pressure and commenting that it is standing by the film (though no details have yet been given).
It is unclear if there has been any communication between ad reps at X and the other social giants. Some other tech firms will also see their leaders under the Hollywood spotlight this fall, with Sony releasing Aaron Sorkin’s Mark Zuckerberg drama The Social Reckoning next month. That film’s trailer is currently available on YouTube.

articles.title_orig: Rogue OpenAI agents accessed US government websites
articles.title_zh: Rogue OpenAI agents accessed US government websites
articles.content_orig:
OpenAI said Friday that some of its AI agents went rogue and probed US government websites this summer — the latest revelation of the artificial intelligence company’s technology.
The New York Times first reported that the AI agents went rogue and attempted to gain access to the Education Department, the Commerce Department and the Securities and Exchange Commission, according to security researchers at AI research lab Transluce.
OpenAI said Saturday that its agents accessed publicly available data from the Commerce Department’s Census Bureau using login credentials it found online, and separately shared public data from the SEC website on another website. OpenAI’s agents attempted but failed to gain access to the Education Department and gather data from its civil rights office, according to the report.
OpenAI told CNN in an email that it notified the agencies of the findings while continuing an “extensive review of misaligned model activity.”
“Most of the activity we’ve reviewed so far involved routine research tasks, such as accessing public web content to answer questions. Some involved government websites because our models often turn to them as authoritative sources of public information,” the spokesperson said.
The Commerce Department, SEC and Education Department did not immediately respond to CNN’s requests for comment.
Rep. Jay Obernolte, the Republican co-chair of the AI caucus, told CNN’s Anderson Cooper on Friday that the incident is “another example of a loss of human control.”
“We need to align the values that these models are trained on with human values, and if we can do that, we can get these models to conform to our standards for human behavior,” he said.
The report comes just days after Australia’s prime minister said that an OpenAI agent hacked into the country’s national healthcare database, marking the first known case of AI hacking a government network. Transluce on Wednesday said that it had detected AI agents going rogue dating back to at least March, unsuccessfully targeting a University of New Mexico library and the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare site.
The Australian website probe occurred in June, an OpenAI spokesperson previously told CNN, but the company was only made aware of it in August.
OpenAI has been investigating agents’ use of internet access since the breach of AI start-up Hugging Face in July.
Sam Altman, OpenAI’s chief executive, said Friday on social media site X that the company was not “as fast as we would have liked.”
“We are trying to balance our desire for transparency with gaining a clear understanding … Hugging Face is still the most severe event we’ve seen,” he wrote .
Competitors Anthropic , Meta and Google have also reported that their agents have gone rogue during breach attempts.
Such breaches have raised alarms within the artificial intelligence community. Tech leaders have jointly called for a slowdown of the technology’s development following Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s essay about “ pacing the frontier ” in mid-September. Amodei warned that people may lose control of AI, which could be misused for “cyberattacks and bioterrorism.”
During the United Nations’ General Assembly on Wednesday, Amodei and Altman urged the UN Security Council to set international standards. Altman said countries need accurate and speedy reporting so that the “world can learn from failures before they become catastrophes.”
Amodei’s warning followed a former Anthropic researcher, Jacob Coxon, whose viral post on X called out AI companies for not acting responsibly with the technology’s development and warned that it “will kill us all.”
AI “doomerism” has faced pushback from tech leaders like Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who said there’s a “0% chance” of the world coming to an end in 2030.
CNN’s Hadas Gold, Hilary Whiteman and Max Saltman contributed to this report.

articles.content_orig:
A quick glance of Saturday's college football schedule show there's no time for apple picking this weekend.
If ever there was a weekend to be locked in front of your television all day, it's this Saturday.
We have six – SIX – top 25 matchups alone. That's more than the first three weeks combined and the most in a single week in three years. College football is like pizza – if you aren't familiar, all pizza is still pretty good – but we still have to celebrate special weekends like this one. We've entered into the part of the season where the games really start to matter.
Like No. 23 Texas A&M at No. 10 LSU. As I wrote earlier this week, that game has all the makings of a loser-leaves-town impact . Both teams started the season as popular College Football Playoff picks and yet one will be 0-2 in conference play before even getting out of September. The data set is small but no team has ever started 0-2 in conference play and still made the playoff.
That's just one of four top 25 SEC matchups.
You can kick the day off with No. 1 Texas at No. 14 Tennessee at noon ET. Is Arch Manning the guy we saw triumphantly guide the Longhorns to a second-half comeback over Ohio State or the guy who struggled against UTSA ? It's a big game for Manning and a star-making opportunity for Tennessee true freshman quarterback Faizon Brandon .
No. 4 Ole Miss at No. 21 Florida might be the most intriguing game of the day. Fresh off a win over former coach Lane Kiffin, will Ole Miss suffer from an emotional hangover, or are the Rebels so good it doesn't matter? First-year head coach Pete Golding is saying all the right things, but escaping from The Swamp with a victory won't be easy. Having a guy like Trinidad Chambliss certainly helps, though.
Kamario Taylor , the other star quarterback in the state of Mississippi, gets a chance to keep the momentum going for No. 24 Mississippi State against No. 19 Missouri . A win over the Tigers would make the Bulldogs 4-0 headed into a huge home game against No. 8 Alabama .
Outside the SEC, we have two tasty Big Ten top-25 games. No. 17 Iowa travels to No. 18 Michigan in what could be a race to see which team can score 20 points first. Both teams sit on the periphery of the CFP race and could take a big step forward with a win on Saturday.
And then there is No. 20 Oregon at No. 12 USC. The Ducks, a popular preseason title pick for some, already have a bad loss to Oklahoma State and can't afford to drop to 2-2 with what's still left on the schedule. Oregon coach Dan Lanning has already faced criticism for his coordinator hires, and that noise will only get louder with a loss in Los Angeles. For Lincoln Riley, it's time to prove the investment was worth it. The Trojans have a chance to make a real statement at home against Oregon and can't let that opportunity slip by.
Noon on ABC, Fubo (try free): After watching its dramatic comeback against Ohio State , Texas looks like a legitimate national title contender, and this line is under a touchdown. That makes it tempting to pick the Longhorns, but the Volunteers remain a mystery. Their game against Georgia Tech was over rather early, so it's hard to gauge exactly what to expect from that squad. Because of that, the total is more appealing. I documented Manning's road struggles above, and I have to give the edge to the Texas defense in a matchup against a true freshman. Points may be at a premium for much of this game. Pick: Under 55.5
3:30 p.m. on ABC, Fubo (try free): I'm a little skeptical of Florida being a favorite in this game, but I've no real interest in going after the spread here. No, the one thing I'm most confident about is that points will be scored. Florida's defense hasn't exactly been incredible despite playing a relatively easy schedule overall, and we've already seen Ole Miss allow points to Louisville and LSU . I think we get another shootout here. Pick: Over 58.5 -- Tom Fornelli
3:30 p.m. on CBS CBSSports.com , CBS Sports App Paramount+ Premium : Michigan has been living on borrowed time the entire season, including the stunning Hail Mary against Western Michigan . Iowa will be the team to finally make them pay -- and ironically, it'll start on offense. Running back Kamari Moulton and wide receiver Tony Diaz give the program one of its best RB-WR combos of the past 20 years, and they will make just enough explosive plays to pull off the upset in the Big House. Pick: Iowa SU (+178) -- Shehan Jeyarajah
3:30 p.m. on ESPN, Fubo (try free): The only quarterbacks in the Power Four more efficient than Gunner Stockton right now are Trinidad Chambliss at Ole Miss and Miami's Darian Mensah -- and no one's talking about the Georgia signal caller's electric start. And when you have one leader on offense in rhythm while the other team's guy is struggling this season from a confidence standpoint, it raises questions about Oklahoma's ability to hang in this matchup. This feels like a 31-7 type game unless the Sooners can get something going offensively for the first time all season against an opponent of substance. Pick: Under 43.5 points -- Brad Crawford
7:30 p.m. on ESPN, Fubo (try free): On the heels of an embarrassing home loss to Kentucky , Texas A&M is venturing into college football's most intimidating night atmosphere. It's the wrong place to be for a team that is grappling with shaky quarterback play. LSU has plenty of flaws, too, but the Tigers are salty enough defensively to make life hard on Marcel Reed . On the other side, A&M's defense never looked comfortable or disruptive against Kentucky. LSU coach Lane Kiffin should have a field day game-planning after watching that tape. Pick: LSU -7.5 -- David Cobb

And while the oddsmakers have clearly identified the strength advantage for both teams, predicting a high-scoring game with their over-under total, it might still not be enough points. These two teams combined for 69 points in 2025 and 63 points in 2023, leaving some wiggle room with the current posted total. Pick: Over 61.5 -- Chip Patterson
